title: Why you need to start planning for a 40-year retirement
full_text:
Australians are older, richer and healthier than ever before. So, when it comes to retirement, is 40 the new 30?
We already know financial advisers assume their clients will be retired for at least 30 years, and potentially longer.
New research suggests Australians may need to start thinking not only about retirement lasting longer than they expect, but also that the path to retirement may look different.
According to Challenger, an Australian couple, both aged 65, have a 43 per cent probability of at least one partner living to 95.
At the same time, Australians who retire due to illness or injury do so at an average age of just 57, seven years earlier than those who retire voluntarily at 64. That means more of us are looking at spending 40 years working, and another 40 in retirement.
“A 40-year retirement isn’t an outlier. For many households it’s a realistic planning case,” Challenger head of retirement income research Aaron Minney said.
“Planning for a longer life doesn’t mean spending less today. It means building a plan that still works if you live longer than you expect.”
When to de-risk your super
Yet as we eye 30- and 40-year retirements, some super funds, including megafund Australian Retirement Trust, are de-risking members from as early as 50 years old, with retirement savings gradually moved from high-risk to a mix of a balanced strategy and cash.
Another major fund to embrace the lifestage investing strategy, Aware Super, starts de-risking its members from 55.
Deloitte partner Andrew Boal said it was worth asking if de-risking in your 50s was too early.
“De-risking has become a risk in itself as we live longer,” Mr Boal said.
He sees merit in gradually moving into lower-risk investments in retirement, but says it’s crucial to get the starting point right.
“If you start at 70 per cent invested in growth and in your mid-50s start de-risking that down (to an end point of) 30 per cent, I think that’s too early and too quickly,” Mr Boal said.
“What we’re seeing now with a number of industry funds (that use a 70/30 investment split) is they’re realising they’re not starting high enough.
“When someone’s in their 20s and 30s, they should be 95 per cent in growth assets, not 70. If your starting point is 95 per cent in growth assets, then starting to de-risk in your mid-50s is OK.”
By the time a retiree is in their 60s, they should have 70 per cent of their super in growth assets and 30 per cent in defensive, and by the 70s this should reduce again down to 50/50, he said.
“The one way to guarantee running out of money if you’ve got a 40-year retirement is to invest too conservatively,” Mr Boal warned.
Easing into retirement
Even moving into retirement is changing, as more of us choose to go part-time for a few years before fully leaving the workforce.
Others face redundancy in their mid-to-late 50s and may struggle to stay in the workforce, meaning retirement comes earlier than expected.
Martha Deevy, an associate director at the US Stanford Centre on Longevity, said traditional expectations around education, career and then retirement were developed for a different time, when we didn’t live as long as we do now.
“That three-stage life no longer works. Today, we should expect several career transitions, some planned, like a gap year, sabbatical, caregiving, education or reskilling, and some unwelcome and costly, like a redundancy,” she said.
AI-driven redundancies are a clear example of such changes that we need to plan for as normal events, Ms Deevy added.
The longevity challenge
Longevity is one of the greatest challenges when planning for retirement.
The major fear among pre-retirees and retirees is running out of money. So the instinct, then, is to spend as little as possible, even in the early years when we are healthy and active.
Mr Boal said longevity products such as annuities could be useful, giving people confidence and certainty there’ll still be some money there in later life.
He said a good age to start looking at annuities was between 65 to 75.
“Many people won’t realise the value of a lifetime income product until they get to that age. By then, they’re working part-time or they’ve stopped working and see what they have left and that they have to make it last for, say, 35 years,” he said.
“You don’t really think about that until you’re relying on it.”
The appeal of annuities is also that some of these products essentially give retirees access to more age pension. This is because 40 per cent of the value of certain annuities is exempt from the means test. No wonder they’re becoming more popular with financial advisers.
